articles.title: A tempestade perfeita (dentro e fora do Brasil) que fez dólar chegar a R$ 6 | G1
articles.standfirst: Pressão fiscal no Brasil e dólar forte no exterior ajudam a explicar a maior desvalorização do real entre as principais moedas emergentes.
articles.summary: Pressão fiscal no Brasil e dólar forte no exterior ajudam a explicar a maior desvalorização do real entre as principais moedas emergentes.
articles.body:
A tempestade perfeita (dentro e fora do Brasil) que faz preço do dólar chegar a R$ 6. — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Depois de liderar as perdas entre as principais moedas de mercados emergentes desde o fim de outubro, o real voltou a se desvalorizar nesta segunda-feira (23/11) chegando a um patamar simbólico: o dólar atingiu R$ 6 pela primeira vez de sde abril de 2025 .

Para analistas, a disparada da moeda americana é resultado de uma combinação de fatores internos e externos que se reforçam mutuamente, formando uma espécie de "tempestade perfeita" para o câmbio brasileiro.

No Brasil, investidores acompanham a análise e a votação do pacote de ajuste fiscal, escrito pelo ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti, na Câmara dos Deputados, prevista para esta segunda – o projeto é uma resposta do governo federal à pressão do mercado financeiro pelo crescimento da dívida pública.

No exterior, o fortalecimento da moeda americana, impulsionado pelas expectativas sobre os juros nos Estados Unidos, pela busca de investimentos considerados mais seguros e pela oscilação dos preços internacionais das commodities, aumenta a pressão sobre moedas de países emergentes.

A desvalorização do real ganhou intensidade a partir do fim de outubro, após o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais.

Desde 25 de outubro, quando o dólar estava cotado a R$ 4,97, até esta segunda, o real havia perdido mais de 16% de seu valor frente à moeda americana , segundo levantamento da BBC News Brasil com as 20 moedas mais utilizadas no comércio exterior. Era a maior desvalorização entre as divisas analisadas.

O mais recente boletim Focus (levantamento feito pelo Banco Central) divulgado nesta segunda mostra que os agentes de mercado esperam que o dólar vai fechar o ano cotado em R$ 5,55 - mas a moeda já chegou a mais de 7% acima deste patamar.

Mas as expectativas do mercado vêm se deteriorando. Há quatro semanas, o levantamento mostrava uma projeção de que o dólar terminaria o ano cotado a R$ 5,13.

Um pacote fiscal que não convenceu o mercado

Segundo economistas ouvidos pela reportagem, o principal fator interno é a percepção de que o governo ainda não apresentou uma solução capaz de enfrentar o crescimento estrutural das despesas públicas.

"Com a reeeleição do presidente Lula para um novo mandato, o mercado ajustou suas expectativas e passou a temer um cenário em que a questão fiscal não fosse devidamente encaminhada", diz Antonio Madeira, economista da consultoria 4intelligence.

Nesse sentido, afirma, o plano de ajuste do governo não está sendo suficiente para conter a desvalorização do real.

O chamado Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) 299/2026, de autoria de Moretti, foi aprovado pelo Senado na quarta-feira (18/11), e a expectativa é que o texto seja votado ainda nesta segunda na Câmara.

Com o objetivo de cortar despesas e aumentar receitas, estima-se que o projeto tenha impacto entre R$ 43 bilhões e R$ 54 bilhões.

Segundo Madeira, o pacote em discussão se concentra principalmente no orçamento do próximo ano, mas deixa em aberto questões ligadas ao avanço das despesas obrigatórias, como Previdência e programas sociais. Isso alimenta preocupações sobre o comportamento futuro da dívida pública e aumenta a percepção de risco entre investidores.

"Hoje, avaliamos que as medidas vão na direção correta, mas, para melhorar as expectativas de forma mais duradoura, seria importante avançar em ajustes estruturais, com foco na trajetória das despesas públicas", diz Luíza Pinese, economista da XP.

Ministro Bruno Moretti, do Planejamento, ao centro, é o autor da primeira proposta de ajuste fiscal do governo Lula após a eleição — Foto: Agência Senado via BBC

Luiz Felipe Vital, chefe de Estratégia Macro e Dívida Pública da Warren Investimentos, faz um diagnóstico semelhante.

"A leitura do mercado, até então, é de que a medida é positiva, mas está muito aquém do que se esperava e de uma medida capaz de estabilizar a dívida pública", avalia.

Declarações de membros da base do governo e de grupos da esquerda, que atacaram a iniciativa dizendo que ela atendia a interesses do mercado financeiro e defenderam um pacote "antiajuste", também contribuem para uma visão mais pessimista do mercado.

Da mesma forma, afirma, a dificuldade de aprovação de um plano considerado modesto diante do tamanho do desafio fiscal brasileiro aumenta a tensão.

E a desconfiança dos investidores em relação ao cenário fiscal acaba pressionando diretamente o câmbio.

Em momentos de maior incerteza e aversão ao risco, investidores tendem a reduzir sua exposição a ativos de mercados emergentes, considerados mais arriscados, e direcionar recursos para mercados e investimentos vistos como mais seguros.

Esse movimento pode provocar saída de capital de países como o Brasil, aumentar a demanda por dólares e exercer pressão adicional sobre o real.

"O investidor vai buscar proteção no dólar ou vai buscar posição direcional no dólar, justamente por esse sentimento de desconfiança", explica o economista da Warren Investimentos.

O cenário internacional também pressiona o câmbio

Além do componente doméstico, o cenário externo também tem contribuído para o fortalecimento da moeda americana.

Nas últimas semanas, investidores passaram a incorporar a possibilidade de que o Federal Reserve (Fed), o banco central dos Estados Unidos, mantenha os juros elevados por mais tempo diante da persistência da inflação americana.

Juros mais altos tornam os ativos americanos mais atraentes e costumam favorecer a valorização do dólar frente a outras moedas.

"A perspectiva de novas altas de juros pelo Fed fortaleceu o dólar ante as principais moedas e elevou os juros dos títulos americanos, o que reduz a atratividade relativa dos ativos de países emergentes", aponta Luíza Pinese, da XP.

Também pesa sobre o real o enfraquecimento dos preços de algumas das principais commodities exportadas pelo Brasil, como o petróleo e o minério de ferro.

Preços mais baixos desses produtos significam menor entrada de dólares na economia brasileira.

Em 2025, o petróleo foi o principal produto exportado pelo Brasil, enquanto o minério de ferro ficou em terceiro lugar, atrás da soja.

Também pesa sobre o real o enfraquecimento dos preços de algumas das principais commodities exportadas pelo Brasil, como o petróleo. — Foto: EPA/Shutterstock via BBC

No caso do petróleo, o preço do barril tipo Brent, que é referência no mercado internacional, iniciou a semana em queda na noite de domingo (22/11), chegando a ser negociado a US$ 89,36, em meio à sequência de altas nos volumes de petróleo bruto armazenados nos Estados Unidos.

Já a queda do minério de ferro vem se intensificando desde o terceiro trimestre de 2026, especialmente a partir de setembro, diante de uma combinação de enfraquecimento da demanda chinesa por aço e aumento da oferta mundial.

Outro fator citado pelos analistas e que ajuda a formar a tempestade que afeta o câmbio brasileiro é o aumento global da aversão ao risco.

Esse movimento ganha força especialmente em meio à incerteza no setor de tecnologia e a uma onda de vendas de ações de empesas do ramo, especialmente as ligadas à inteligência artificial.

"Em momentos de aumento da aversão ao risco, as moedas de países emergentes acabam por sofrer também", diz Antonio Madeira, da 4intelligence.

A pressão sobre o real também costuma se intensificar no fim do ano por razões sazonais, apontam os especialistas. Nesse período, empresas aumentam a demanda por dólares para remessas ao exterior, pagamento de dívidas e fechamento de posições financeiras.

Para tentar equilibrar um mercado considerado disfuncional, o Banco Central interveio -- primeiro por meio de leilão de linha e depois vendendo dólares diretamente no mercado à vista, operação que não ocorria desde dezembro de 2024.

Mas na avaliação dos economistas ouvidos pela BBC News Brasil, intervenções desse tipo até podem reduzir a volatilidade no curto prazo, mas dificilmente alteram a trajetória do câmbio quando os fundamentos econômicos continuam apontando para uma moeda brasileira mais fraca.

"Nosso Banco Central ele não atua para defender o nível ou para fazer pressão no sentido contrário na taxa, mas atua para manter o mercado funcional", diz Luiz Felipe Vital.

Por todos esses fatores, os economistas ouvidos pela BBC News Brasil avaliam que a aprovação do pacote fiscal do governo Lula dificilmente será suficiente para reverter, sozinha, a pressão sobre o câmbio.

Para Antonio Madeira, enquanto persistir a preocupação dos investidores com a trajetória a longo prazo das contas públicas, o prêmio de risco do país deve permanecer elevado, limitando uma recuperação mais forte do real mesmo em momentos de alívio nos mercados internacionais.

Segundo ele, a preocupação dos investidores não está restrita ao orçamento de 2027, mas à capacidade de o país conter o avanço das despesas obrigatórias nos próximos anos.

Luíza Pinese, da XP, ressalta que os indicadores de risco do Brasil já se aproximam dos níveis de episódios anteriores de estresse, o que deixa menos espaço para piora.

"A direção do câmbio dependerá sobretudo da credibilidade fiscal doméstica e da trajetória dos juros nos Estados Unidos", aponta.

Já Luis Felipe Vital, da Warren, tem uma visão mais otimista. Para o economista, a capacidade do governo de demonstrar compromisso com medidas adicionais de ajuste fiscal nos próximos meses é central.

Mas com tempo e uma contínua sinalização do governo sobre seu comprometimento com os gastos públicos, ainda que dentro das limitações políticas, pode haver uma retomada do real.

"O governo vai ter que trabalhar com uma sequência de medidas e com sinalizações até que o mercado entenda que existe um plano construtivo, que pode não atendê-lo na velocidade que gostaria, mas que vai fazer um ajuste nas contas que em algum momento vai se mostrar suficiente para manter uma estabilidade econômica", diz.

articles.title: Sensex slides 1,484 points as global market weakness weighs on D-Street investors
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Global AI-led market sell-off got the better of Dalal Street's month-long foreign funds-led rally on Monday with the sensex closing 1,484-point
articles.body: MUMBAI: Global AI-led market sell-off got the better of Dalal Street's month-long foreign funds-led rally on Monday with the sensex closing 1,484-point down at 82,436 points. Profit taking by local traders after nearly a 15% gain in the last one month also helped the slide in the indices, market players said.Selling was concentrated in banking and financial services, metal and select energy stocks while Indian IT stocks, which are now being considered safe havens from the global AI-led sell-off, saw some smart up moves, they said. The day's session also left investors poorer by a little over Rs 5 lakh crore with the combined market capitalisation of companies listed on the BSE now at Rs 509 lakh crore, exchange data showed. On NSE, nifty lost 451 points or 1.8% to close at 25,350 points. During Monday's session, sensex opened higher but soon entered the negative territory and eventually slid over 2,200 points from the day's high as selling picked up pace.Of the 30 sensex stocks, 22 closed in the red. Among these, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Axis bank contributed the most to the index's loss in the day.On BSE, bankex, the banking sector index lost 3.1% while on NSE, nifty bank index closed 3.2% down.According to Vinod Nair, head of research, Geojit Investments, last week's late global sell-off, triggered by concerns over an AI bubble and tighter US monetary policy, weighed on Indian equities on Monday. On Friday night in the US, Nasdaq Composite index had crashed 5.3% while S& slid 3.7% and Dow Jones index was down 2%."Global cues remained fragile, with Asian markets tracking Friday's sharp sell-off in the US technology stocks. Concerns over elevated AI valuations, the sustainability of AI-led capital expenditure and the unwinding of crowded technology positions continued to erode risk appetite, spilling over into domestic equities and reinforcing a cautious trading environment," added Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, a wealth-tech platform. Indian markets are closed on Tuesday for Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev, BSE said on its website.The day's 1.8% slide in sensex came despite a Rs 5,673-crore net buying by foreign funds. So far this month, foreign portfolio investors have net pumped in nearly Rs 1.4 lakh crore into Indian equities, combined data from NSDL and BSE showed. During Monday's session, domestic funds were net sellers with the net outflow at Rs 2,760 crore, BSE data showed.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: IDBI not govt bank: SC; staff interest protected: Centre
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Supreme Court has held that IDBI is not a \"State\" within Article 12 of Constitution, which means it was not a govt entity, dealing a blow
articles.body: New Delhi: The Supreme Court has held that IDBI is not a "State" within Article 12 of Constitution, which means it was not a govt entity, dealing a blow to the the bank's officer's association, even as govt maintained that the interests of employees and pensioners of the bank have been fully protected.Last week, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran dismissed an appeal filed against a 2022 decision of the Bombay High Court, which struck down demand of the association, that called for retirement and provident fund benefits for employees of United Western Bank, which had merged with IDBI, arguing that the Centre retained administrative, functional and financial control over IDBI till 2018 and LIC, which acquired stake in the bank, was also owned and controlled by govt.The SC ruling will also have an implication on the "strategic restructuring" of IDBI Bank, where govt and LIC are selling over 60% stake held by in the bank to Fairfax. Employees have called for scrapping the sale, questioning the valuation and arguing that benchmarking it to public sector stock was not proper as IDBI is a private bank. Govt has also allayed concerns over retirement and salary benefits.When contacted, DIPAM secretary Arunish Chawla said: "Govt and LIC are not employers under the Labour Code. IDBI Bank is the employer under the Code. A strategic transaction is executed through a share purchase agreement within the framework of the Contract Law. DIPAM appoints transaction and legal advisers, who in turn consult with the qualified parties on the one hand and with the bank management on the other. IDBI is a board-run banking company and management consults the employees internally, and has in this case presented a very robust protection framework for employees and pensioners, which is the best ever granted in such transactions. The service conditions of existing employees cannot be changed, modified or altered to their disadvantage after the strategic restructuring. The IDBI management has made sure all the service rules framed by the board are included in the annexures to the draft agreement. The pensioners are also fully protected, there is a special fund for it and their pension benefits will be full honoured."Asked about the controversy over valuation of two properties, Chawla said Cuffe Parade headquarters in Mumbai was on 60-year lease and valuation was based on the rental saving for the remaining 25 years of lease. In the case of the training centre in Hyderabad, the property cannot be transferred in the open market and comparing its value to market-auctioned property would have been "absurd".Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Stock market holiday today: Are BSE, NSE closed on November 24 for Guru Nanak Jayanti?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The BSE and NSE will remain closed on Tuesday, November 24, on account of Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev or Guru Nanak Jayanti.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BSE and NSE will remain closed on Tuesday, November 24, on account of Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev or Guru Nanak Jayanti. Commodity trading on the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX), however, will resume during the evening session.This is the second-last stock market holiday of 2026, with the final one scheduled for December 25 on account of Christmas.Why are NSE and BSE closed today?The National Stock Exchange (NSE) and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) have declared November 24 a trading holiday for Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev, also known as Guru Nanak Jayanti.Trading will remain suspended across the equity, equity derivatives, securities lending and borrowing (SLB), capital market, derivatives market, electronic gold receipts (EGR) and debt market segments.The MCX will follow a partial trading schedule, with its morning session closed from 9 am to 5 pm. Trading will resume in the evening session from 5 pm to 11.30 pm.The National Commodity and Derivatives Exchange (NCDEX) will remain closed for the entire day.The holiday comes after a sharp sell-off in domestic equities on Monday, with both benchmark indices declining nearly 1.8% amid heavy selling in banking and metal stocks, weakness in global markets and profit booking following the recent rally.The Nifty 50 closed at 25,349.65, down 450.95 points or 1.75%, while the BSE Sensex settled at 82,435.99, declining 1,483.72 points or 1.77%.Selling pressure was broad-based, with banking and commodity stocks bearing the brunt of the decline. The Nifty Bank index fell more than 3% to 62,585 after recently touching an all-time high, while the Nifty Metal index recorded the steepest sectoral decline, shedding 3.70%.The Nifty IT index was the only major sectoral index to close in positive territory, gaining 1.8%.When will stock market trading resume?Trading on the NSE and BSE will resume on Wednesday, November 25, with regular market hours. The MCX will also operate its regular morning and evening sessions on Wednesday, while the NCDEX will resume trading after the holiday.The next and final scheduled stock market holiday of the year will be December 25 for Christmas, apart from regular weekend closures.Global markets rebound after Wall Street rallyAsian shares surged on Tuesday following a strong rally on Wall Street, as technology and AI-related stocks rebounded sharply after recent losses.MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan climbed 4.6%, recovering from an eight-month low and heading for its biggest single-day gain in two weeks.Japan's Nikkei rose 4.5% as traders returned after a local holiday, while South Korea's KOSPI surged 7.5% and Taiwanese shares jumped 9.1%.Nvidia shares rallied 31.5% on Monday, marking their biggest daily percentage gain in 23 years and restoring nearly $1 trillion in market value. The rally also lifted other AI-related stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 jumping more than 6%.The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite surged 4.7% and 6.5%, respectively, while S&P 500 futures were flat and Nasdaq futures edged down 0.2% early on Tuesday.Brent crude futures were flat at $89.50 a barrel after settling 3.5% lower at $89.37 on Monday. Gold also recovered from a more than one-year low, with spot prices rising 0.7% to $3,657.97 an ounce as investors bought the dip.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: Moonrider deploys nearly 100 electric tractors, counts Reliance among clients
articles.summary: Moonrider has deployed nearly 100 electric tractors, including at Reliance CBG sites, offering 27-75 HP models and claiming up to 75% lower operating costs.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Electric tractor startup Moonrider has deployed nearly 100 vehicles across agricultural and industrial applications, including at Reliance’s compressed biogas (CBG) facilities, as it looks to expand the use of battery-powered tractors beyond conventional farming.Prashanth N, a member of Moonrider’s founding team, told TOI at the Bengaluru Tech Summit that the company was serving both institutional customers and individual farmers in Karnataka.Founded in 2023 by Anoop Srikantaswamy and Ravi Kulkarni, Bengaluru-based Moonrider manufactures electric tractors in three horsepower categories: 27 HP, 50 HP and 75 HP.Its entry-level 27 HP model, equipped with a 24 kWh battery, starts at Rs 7.9 lakh and targets farmers. The 50 HP tractor, designed for heavier agricultural and industrial work, costs around Rs 14 lakh, while the 75 HP model is expected to cost approximately Rs 20 lakh.Prashanth said customers could save up to 75% in operating costs compared with conventional diesel tractors.Moonrider raised $6 million in Series A funding in December 2025, led by pi Ventures, with participation from Singularity AMC and existing investors AdvantEdge Founders and Micelio Technology Fund. It had earlier raised $2.2 million in seed funding in January 2025.The company designs its own electric powertrains, battery packs and vehicle electronics. Its tractors are intended for activities ranging from tilling and hauling to material movement at industrial facilities.In September, Moonrider also entered into a partnership with BikeWo Green Tech to explore electric tractor deployments, leasing and fleet operations across commercial and institutional applications.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: From a Himalayan village to building a cybersecurity giant: Jay Chaudhry’s remarkable journey
articles.summary: Jay Chaudhry’s journey from a Himalayan village to founding Zscaler, now in a $43B CrowdStrike deal, highlighting his startups, IPO and cloud security rise.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Even as the cybersecurity industry witnesses a mega-deal, with CrowdStrike acquiring Zscaler in a $43 billion transaction, the story of Zscaler founder and serial tech entrepreneur Jay Chaudhry is a reminder of how extraordinary dreams can take root in the most unlikely places — even on a farm.Born into a family of small farmers in a tiny village in the foothills of the Himalayas, on the Punjab-Himachal Pradesh border, about 30 km from the Bhakra Nangal dam, Chaudhry grew up with few of the amenities that urban India took for granted. “Our village got electricity when I finished 8th grade, running water when I finished 10th grade. I sat in a car for the first time after 12th grade. And I had a flight for the first time when I went to America to do my Master’s,” he told TOI in an interview in 2020.His parents encouraged him to study because they had not had the opportunity themselves. His father had dropped out after Class 5 because the nearest middle school was too far away to walk to.Chaudhry was academically gifted, and his teachers took an interest in him. He recalls one teacher in Class 10 telling him: “You’re wasting your time in the class. Go and sit in those bushes and read. Come back, do your assignments and show me your assignments twice a day.”For pre-university (Class 11), he joined a college at the district headquarters, about 12 km away, a distance he would cover by bicycle. He went on to become a gold medallist at Himachal University. He initially considered studying engineering at Punjab Engineering College, but a teacher told him about the IITs and their system of admitting top performers from universities.“I didn’t even know about the IITs then,” Chaudhry said.He applied for electronics engineering and secured admission to IIT-BHU. Moving from a village in Himachal Pradesh to the metropolitan environment of BHU was a cultural shock, but he adapted. With many students talking about pursuing higher studies in the US, he too applied during his final year.The University of Cincinnati, Ohio, offered him a tuition scholarship. A Tata scholarship programme for students going abroad helped him fund his airline ticket.“It was just luck and it comes together sometimes,” he said modestly.Chaudhry earned a Master’s degree in computer engineering and another in industrial engineering from the University of Cincinnati, where he also met his wife, Jyoti, an MBA graduate from IIM Calcutta. He later worked at IBM and a few other companies before deciding to strike out on his own.The internet boom of the 1990s had spawned a wave of successful startups, and Chaudhry wanted to build a company in internet security. But finding funding proved difficult. One day, Jyoti confronted him: “Hey, you keep talking about it (starting a venture). Either you do something or you shut up.”Chaudhry told her that the only way to get started was to put their life savings into the venture. Jyoti brought a combination of technology and finance expertise to the table. The two decided to take the risk and jointly founded SecureIT in 1996.“It was probably the biggest and best gamble of our lives,” he says.Within two years, SecureIT was acquired by VeriSign for $70 million. The Atlanta-based venture became a success story, with 70 of its 80 employees becoming millionaires.With the proceeds from the sale, the couple went on to establish three more startups in quick succession, all of which were acquired. Chaudhry’s entrepreneurial journey included AirDefense, a wireless security pioneer acquired by Motorola; CipherTrust, which he founded in 2000 and led until its merger with Secure Computing in 2006; and CoreHarbor, a managed ecommerce solutions company acquired by USi/AT&T.By 2007, he was looking to build “something big, something special, something lasting”. Having watched software-as-a-service companies such as Salesforce and NetSuite gain traction, he became convinced that security, too, would have to move to the cloud. That conviction led to the founding of Zscaler in 2008.Zscaler went public on March 16, 2018, and has since emerged as a major player in cloud security, with customers including GE, Siemens and Shell.Chaudhry recalled meeting Jim Fowler, then CIO of GE, in 2019. “I said, Jim, thank you for making time to see me, even though we are such a small fraction of your IT budget. He smiled and said, ‘Even though you’re a small part of the budget, without Zscaler, I have no cloud strategy. I want you to come and see me every six months.’”Chaudhry and his family have a 34% stake in Zscaler. The CrowdStrike acquisition values that stake at nearly $15 billion.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: SpaceX-Tesla: The directors negotiating the biggest merger ever
articles.summary: SpaceX and Tesla have entrusted five directors with the fate of the largest merger of all time, with the quintet hashing out the terms of a potential...
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) have entrusted five directors with the fate of the largest merger of all time, with the quintet hashing out the terms of a potential $3.5tn combination and racing to complete the deal before the end of the year.

Elon Musk's two public companies have appointed a handful of directors — three from Tesla and two from SpaceX — deemed financially "disinterested" to guide two special committees handling merger negotiations.

Those directors are Roelof Botha and Randy Glein from SpaceX and Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung from Tesla, according to people close to the process.

All five have longstanding ties to Musk and face a difficult task to map out how the two sprawling businesses could be brought together, win over shareholders and protect themselves from investor lawsuits that have plagued previous dealmaking by the billionaire's companies.

"They can't afford to let Elon bulldoze them. They need to do this by the book," one of the people said.

Special committees are standard practice for conflicted deals, but this process is unique with both sides sharing a chief executive, who is also the world's richest man.

The special committees have hired advisers — including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs for SpaceX and Evercore for Tesla — who are fine-tuning financial models that will form the basis for their negotiating positions in an all-stock merger, the people said.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. Botha declined to comment. Tesla, SpaceX and Evercore did not respond to written requests for comment.

The bankers are examining which parts of the proposed conglomerate overlap , such as AI models, chip-design efforts and data centres — while identifying complementary "synergies" that could include rockets, robotics and solar panels, the people said.

The two sides must then hammer out a fair "exchange ratio" for SpaceX and Tesla shares. This will be closely watched by institutional investors as well as Musk's army of retail shareholders, who hold an estimated 20 per cent of the electric vehicle maker and are very bullish on the company's valuation.

"There is more friction than people assume. I don't think the committees are close yet," one of the people said. "But the culture of Elon's companies is to work 24 hours a day, seven days a week and then execute immediately."

"It could get done before the end of the year," they added.

If the financial terms can be settled, the companies will hash out governance rights and who takes crucial roles in the merged entity, including whether there is a chair, who will be chief financial officer and which directors will remain. "Elon will decide that and decide it quickly," said one person. "No one is under any illusions: this is his company."

articles.title: Is US headed for recession? Falling household wealth, market turmoil put pressure on economy
articles.summary: Is the US economy heading towards a recession, or is the recent stock market selloff a temporary bout of panic?
articles.body: Is the US economy heading towards a recession, or is the recent stock market selloff a temporary bout of panic? An assessment by Ionic Wealth puts the probability of a recession at 25%, while assigning a 75% chance to a market correction that eventually reverses.The report identifies simultaneous weakness in three major drivers of household financial strength - wages, equity holdings and home values - as a growing risk to consumer spending. Their decline in real terms during the current quarter could undermine one of the key pillars that has helped the US economy withstand repeated economic shocks.“Recession at 25% and a Panic That Reverses at 75%...Most of the concerns behind the selloff point to an AI build out that takes longer, rather than one that stops. A recession needs the Fed and the consumer to fail together”, the report stated.The housing market is adding to these concerns. Pending home sales dropped 17% year-on-year in October, pointing to weakening activity. Meanwhile, households have a near-record proportion of their financial assets invested in equities, increasing their exposure to market volatility.The scale of the recent correction is reflected in the performance of major US indices. The Nasdaq 100 has shed 19.8% from its October 5 peak, while the S&P 500 is down 11.6% from its October 6 record.The report also flagged the risk of monetary tightening if inflation remains stubbornly high. With inflation at 3.7%, it estimated that the Federal Reserve may have to push interest rates to 6.75% by the end of 2027 to achieve its 2% inflation target. Such a trajectory, it warned, would place considerable strain on consumers and the US Treasury.However, the assessment does not view the stock market decline as evidence of collapsing demand for artificial intelligence. Instead, it points to a possible delay in the pace of investment. Orders for AI infrastructure reportedly stretch into 2028 and 2029, while a large portion of memory capacity has already been booked.This forms the basis of the report's more optimistic outlook, which sees the current market turmoil subsiding as AI-related demand holds up and the Federal Reserve softens its policy stance after December. It assigns this outcome a 75% probability.The more pessimistic scenario, with a 25% probability, hinges on the Federal Reserve continuing to raise rates through 2027 even as household finances deteriorate. The combination could weaken consumption enough to push the economy into recession.The report identified the Fed's next policy moves as a crucial indicator, arguing that a shift in its stance before further damage to household wealth and spending could help prevent a deeper economic downturn.The next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) policy decision is scheduled for December 9, following its December 8-9 meeting.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Why is gas suddenly cheaper? Five factors driving the drop to $3.64 a gallon
articles.summary: A combination of geopolitical, seasonal, and operational factors are pushing fuel prices lower heading into the holiday season.
articles.body:
The average price of gasoline in the U.S. has plunged nearly 90 cents a gallon in two months down to its lowest level since the early days of the Iran war, coming just in time for Thanksgiving travel.

Context, of course, matters. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday. Though that's 57 cents higher than the price a year ago, according to AAA, it has come down precipitously of late. And it would only hace to fall a bit further to $3.58 to hit where it stood on Thanksgiving Day 2022. Over the weekend, in some parts of the country, prices at the pump could be seen hovering at—or occasionally even below—the $3 mark, a huge psychological break for consumers who have suffered through years of rising prices.

"The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. "But, given how things have developed, it's not really a shock."

So, why have prices fallen so sharply since late September? It's a combination of geopolitical factors in the Middle East, typical seasonal declines, and refinery operational issues. And, no, there wasn't any conspiracy to keep prices higher ahead of the midterm elections. However, President Donald Trump's actions are key contributors.

Here are the five main factors causing fuel prices—especially gasoline—to tumble:

More oil exports are exiting the Middle East, including from the now-infamous Strait of Hormuz

Despite some ongoing conflict, the combination of U.S. naval escorts, complicated oil tanker transfers, and pipeline bypass routes have allowed the Middle East to return to nearly 90% of its pre-war oil exports, even though prices remain elevated from high tanker contracting and insurance costs. The rising levels of oil exports—despite depleted strategic oil reserves worldwide—have helped the global oil benchmark dip slightly below $90 per barrel as of Monday.

Trump has downplayed any large escalation of military conflict since the midterm elections and the blue wave of Democratic wins

Prior to the elections, Trump openly said he was delaying any major ramp-up in attacks until after the midterms. That warning was keeping oil prices inflated as oil markets anticipated more disruptions to global oil flows in November. While risks remain and no peace deal seems on the near-term horizon, the lack of an escalation has helped prices fall. "The biggest thing now is this looming uncertainty over whether there will be something concrete and long-lasting," De Haan told Fortune .

articles.title: AI’s most powerful CEO is back. But how long will the market confidence last?
articles.summary: The magnitude of the market’s moves underpins how critical Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang are to the health of the AI boom.
articles.body: Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia has revived hopes for an AI industry that’s been badly shaken in recent weeks. Since Huang’s departure 11 days ago, Nvidia had shed more than $1 trillion in market value, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite neared the brink of a bear market. Shares of companies involved in the AI buildout — from the neoclouds like CoreWeave to the chipmakers like Micron — dropped sharply. Stocks were rebounding early Monday, but Huang’s return supercharged the rally. The Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5% — its best day in 19 months. The magnitude of the market’s moves underpins how critical Nvidia and its CEO are to the health of the AI boom. Nvidia has been more than just a semiconductor chip designer. The company is at the heart of financing investments across the AI industry. Huang’s return “gives some hope to the idea that Nvidia’s role as the central bank of AI is still intact,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, told CNN. Huang championed much of the AI industry’s financing, and he positioned Nvidia at the center of it all. “Circular financing” or “vendor financing” have emerged as terms to describe Nvidia’s financial agreements, because the company is backing the companies that, in turn, buy its products. Huang had long championed Nvidia’s role in financing infrastructure deals. Now that he’s back, investors are trying to see whether he’ll pick up the pace or face new challenges. “He’s clearly been a big advocate of some pretty aggressive financing policies, and I think those continue, for better or for worse,” Goldberg said. AI’s lender of last resort Huang has been a kingmaker for the AI industry, using Nvidia’s immense balance sheet and revered status to guarantee loans, invest in startups and direct capital to help facilitate the data center buildout. Under Huang, Nvidia also built a substantial venture capital and merger and acquisitions business. The value of its venture capital deals this year hit roughly $220 billion, and M&A deals hit roughly $33 billion, according to data from PitchBook. His short-lived absence put the spotlight on whether the ecosystem he built could exist without him — and whether there would be negative ripple effects across the markets and economy. “Jensen’s return gives investors more confidence that Nvidia can execute the deals it has already put in motion, that without him were clouded,” said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO at Mahoney Asset Management. Wells Fargo equity analysts wrote in a note that Huang’s reinstatement helps answer multiple investor questions and concerns about the “broader AI ecosystem financing support.” Still, there are questions as to whether the recent turmoil will make it more difficult for Huang to act with the same gusto as before. Huang’s actions will be under a spotlight from here on out with potentially more scrutiny than before, analysts noted. “Even before Jensen fell into trouble, there were all kinds of concerns about the viability of the model,” Goldberg at Seaport Research Partners said. “That doesn’t go away.” “There’s still lots of legitimate questions about the business model behind all these data centers, but at least for the moment they get another lease on life,” he added. “They live to fight another day.” Relief and risks Huang’s return caused a sharp rally in the so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave, which rent out compute power for the AI boom and are backed by Nvidia. CoreWeave shares on Friday closed at $39.51, below their IPO price in 2025, and were down 35% since Huang’s initial ousting from Nvidia — a testament to just how much they struggled while Huang was out of his job. “The ability of the U.S. to be able to continue to grow its AI ecosystem, which is driving most of the economy, as of Friday, felt impaired,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson. “With Jensen Huang coming back and really being exonerated by the president, I’d say we’re back in business, and it is likely that Nvidia will continue to fund partners in its ecosystem,” Luria said. CoreWeave shares jumped 22% on Monday, as Huang’s return may have cleared up a lot of uncertainty for investors. Still, it doesn’t address the big-picture concerns about the sustainability of the ecosystem. If demand for AI continues to grow and translates into strong revenue and profits for tech companies, the data center buildout will likely continue to meet that demand and the financing machine can continue. But if growth slows, or investors begin to further scrutinize the cost-benefit analysis of how much money is being spent versus the return on investment, there could be further trouble for the AI boom. That core premise remains with or without Huang at the helm of Nvidia. Nvidia’s stock is not out of the woods, analysts said. Investors still have to reckon with a bevy of questions, from scrutiny from lawmakers to the impact of export controls on sales. It remains to be seen whether Huang can be an AI industry leader in the same manner he was before, but for now the market has rejoiced in his return. “If AI is a modern day gold rush, Nvidia sells the picks, owns shares in the mines, and even acts as the bank that lends to the prospectors,” said Robert Lalka, a professor of business at Tulane University’s Freeman School of Business. “Evidently, Nvidia is too big to fail, and Jensen Huang is too big to fire,” Lalka said.

articles.title: Nvidia's longtime CFO and now former interim CEO Colette Kress was left in the dark about Jensen Huang's return: Report
articles.summary: She has been the CFO of Nvidia (NVDA) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom right alongside founder and public face Jensen Hu...
articles.body:
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang.

She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.

She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.

In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.

And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.

"The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim chief executive officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions," a new report on Tuesday from the Financial Times said, citing people familiar with the matter.

An Nvidia spokesperson didn't respond to Yahoo Finance's request for comment.

Shares of Nvidia fell 5% in early trading on Tuesday after a 31.2% surge on news that founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as CEO. That came just 12 days after he resigned amid a personal scandal and federal chip-export probes.

Kress is returning to the CFO role, though her LinkedIn profile still says interim CEO.

The dramatic reversal followed intense lobbying from President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who intervened directly with directors and said Huang had been cleared of national security concerns.

Upon returning to Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters, Huang promised employees he would be a better CEO the second time around.

Despite the rally , Nvidia still faces ongoing DOJ and SEC investigations into alleged chip smuggling through blacklisted Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, prompting the board to appoint a new chief compliance officer.

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title: Turkey, cranberries and sweet potatoes are all more expensive this Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Thanksgiving prices are on the rise for the first time in four years, with American households expected to pay 6% more than last year.
articles.body: American households are expected to pay more for Thanksgiving staples, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation, marking the first price hike since 2022. The average Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people will cost about $58.63, or $5.86 per person, according to the AFBF’s annual survey. That’s up 6.3% from last year but down from a record high of $64.05 in 2022. AFBF volunteer shoppers check prices the first week of November, before lower prices take effect in the days leading up to Thanksgiving. Turkey, the centerpiece that makes up about 40% of Thanksgiving meal costs, had the largest price increase of all: The average price for a 16-pound frozen turkey is $23.68, up 10% from last year. Cranberries and milk are nearly 9% more expensive, dinner rolls are 7% more expensive and three pounds of sweet potatoes cost 5% more, according to AFBF data. “The increase was not a terrible surprise to us … because we are in an inflated cost environment when it comes to the common denominator for all of these products, and that is the use of diesel,” AFBF economist Cameron Castillo said. Diesel prices are near record highs, with the national average at $5.81 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA. That affects a variety of production costs for farmers, on top of a turkey population recovering from the avian flu, Castillo said. “Even though an American consumer might have to pay more in the grocery store… that should not be misconstrued as an economic benefit for the farmer, the rancher, or the grower,” he said, noting that farmers are bearing the brunt of inflationary pressures. A Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute analysis found that a meal for 10 will cost $78.93 this year, or down 0.4% from a year ago, including dessert. In Wells Fargo’s analysis, turkey prices largely held steady, though some instances of turkey prices are “way up” from last year, according to chief agricultural economist Michael Swanson. Major retailers and manufacturers have shown a willingness to absorb additional costs, Swanson said, because they’re focused on maintaining sales volumes. Thanksgiving on a budget Americans are grappling with rising food costs and other inflationary pressures, with more than 50% of surveyed consumers saying inflation is affecting their plans or budgets, according to a report from financial marketplace LendingTree. And 62% of potential hosts say they may need to borrow, with 18% planning to use buy now, pay later loans. “A holiday meal can be expensive enough on its own. When you add credit card interest or other borrowing costs, that one day of celebrating can end up costing you for months afterward,” said Matt Schulz, LendingTree’s chief consumer finance analyst, in a statement. Families might clip coupons and follow weekly discounts to save money, Castillo said. Major grocers including Walmart, Target and Costco are also offering Thanksgiving meal bundles. At Walmart, a meal for 10 costs about $35, or $3.50 per person, and has 18% more items than last year, including a turkey, corn muffin mix, cans of vegetables and russet potatoes. That’s roughly 12% less expensive than last year. Target’s $30 meal for six includes turkey at 79 cents a pound, in addition to russet potatoes, cranberry sauce, green beans and other items. Last year, its meal was under $20 but included fewer items. Costco, meanwhile, has offered a $200 meal for eight people. That includes 30 pounds of food, from turkey breast to pumpkin pie. As for wealthier spenders, retailers “don’t feel obligated to lower prices or even make much of an effort to give you value,” Swanson said. Retailers know wealthier shoppers want “convenience, flavor, variety, cachet, all those things,” he told CNN. “The market is very, very segmented at this point in time.”

Thanksgiving shopping remains a major tradition for American households, who are shopping around for meal deals to meet their budgets.

articles.title: Year-round tax planning for salaried employees: a 12-month approach explained
articles.summary: By Archit Gupta Every person’s personal finance rests on three things. The first is protecting yourself and your family through life and health insurance.
articles.body: By Archit GuptaEvery person’s personal finance rests on three things. The first is protecting yourself and your family through life and health insurance. The second is your home, and the loan that usually comes with it. The third is building wealth, turning your savings into a corpus that grows over time, whether that corpus is a retirement fund decades away or simply money set aside for a year-end holiday. What ties the three together is that each has a tax side.The insurance you buy, the home loan you service, the investments you choose- every one of them can shape your tax, and deciding on them thoughtfully can leave more money in your hands. That is why tax planning works best not as a year-end scramble in March, but as a steady, year-round discipline woven into these everyday decisions. Here is how a salaried employee can approach it across twelve months.Start with an estimate, in AprilThe foundation of good planning is an early estimate of your liability. At the start of the financial year, add up your expected salary, any income outside it such as interest, rent or capital gains, and the deductions you realistically expect to claim. This one exercise tells you your likely tax for the year, and it is what every later decision rests on. Without it, you are saving and investing blind, and you discover your actual position only when it is too late to change it.An estimate also reveals the size of the decision in front of you. Someone who will owe very little needs to do almost nothing; someone with a larger liability can see exactly how much planning is worth, and plan proportionately.Choose the regime deliberately, not by habitThe most consequential decision is which tax regime to use. The new regime, now the default, offers lower rates across wider slabs but withdraws most deductions. The old regime keeps higher rates but allows house rent allowance, Section 80C investments, health insurance under Section 80D, home-loan interest and more.The practical way to choose is a break-even test: the old regime is cheaper only if your total deductions cross a break-even level, and that level rises with income. Take a salaried person earning around Rs 20 lakh a year. For the old regime to beat the new, they would need roughly Rs 7 lakh of deductions, over and above the standard deduction. At exactly that break-even point, both regimes leave them with the same tax, a little over Rs 1.9 lakh.If their deductions fall short of that, the new regime is cheaper and simpler; if they comfortably exceed it, the old regime pulls ahead. For many salaried people, especially those without a home loan or large Section 80C commitments, reaching that level is difficult, which is why the new regime often works out better by default.The real error is not choosing one regime over the other; it is choosing out of habit without running both sets of numbers on your own income. This decision belongs at the start of the year, not at filing, because the regime you expect to use sets how much tax your employer deducts each month.Align your TDS with realityYour employer deducts tax every month based on the regime and investments you declare, so declaring them early keeps your monthly deductions accurate and your take-home steady. The part that needs your active attention is income your employer cannot see: interest, capital gains or freelance earnings.Where your tax on that, after TDS, is likely to exceed Rs 10,000 for the year, it must be paid as advance tax in instalments across June, September, December and March. Tracking it through the year avoids a last-minute crunch and the interest that comes with missing it.Spread your deductions across the yearThe heart of year-round planning is spreading deductions over twelve months instead of bunching them into March.Under Section 80C, up to Rs 1.5 lakh is deductible. Rather than a single lump sum in March, a monthly contribution, a SIP into an equity-linked savings scheme, or regular provident fund and PPF additions spreads the cost and averages your investment price. Your EPF contribution and your children's tuition fees already count towards this limit.Health insurance, under Section 80D, allows up to Rs 25,000, rising to Rs 50,000 where you insure senior-citizen parents, a separate limit from your own family's cover. Paying premiums when the policy falls due, rather than scrambling in March, keeps both the cover and the deduction intact.The National Pension System offers an additional Rs 50,000 deduction under Section 80CCD(1B), over and above 80C. A small monthly contribution builds this painlessly. Notably, an employer's NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(2) remains available even under the new regime, one of the few benefits that survives it.If you pay rent, keep your rent receipts and your landlord's PAN, which is required where annual rent crosses Rs 1 lakh, through the year rather than reconstructing them at the end. Treated monthly, these choices ease cash flow and, more importantly, get made for sound financial reasons rather than to beat a deadline.Review at the midpointPlans drift. A bonus, a job change, a new source of income or a shift in investments can all move your liability.A single mid-year review, around September or October, lets you correct course: adjust your declared investments, top up a shortfall, or revise your advance-tax estimate while there is still time to act.Do's and don'ts for regime selectionDo run both regimes on your actual numbers before deciding, and decide at the start of the year. Do declare your regime and investments to your employer early. Do keep documentation through the year. Do revisit the decision if your income changes.Don't lock money away or buy insurance purely to save tax; the deduction should follow a genuine need, not drive it. Don't leave the regime to default or habit without checking. Don't wait for March, when rushed proofs and hurried investments are exactly where costly mistakes are made. And don't overlook income outside your salary, which can quietly trigger advance tax.Done steadily, tax planning stops being stressful. It turns a deadline into a routine, aligns your tax with your actual financial life, and usually leaves more money in your hands. The best time to begin is the first month of the financial year, not the last.(The author is Founder and CEO, ClearTax)Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: Trump could have gained up to $15 million from Nvidia rally after Huang’s return
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s holdings in chipmaker Nvidia may have gained as much as $15 million in value, according to his latest financial disclosures,
articles.body: US President Donald Trump’s holdings in chipmaker Nvidia may have gained as much as $15 million in value, according to his latest financial disclosures, as cited by the Financial Times.The potential gain came after Nvidia shares surged more than 30 per cent on Monday following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as its chief executive.Trump’s financial filings with the Office of Government Ethics, the most recent of which was submitted on November 5, indicate that he may have held as many as 370,000 Nvidia shares as of September 30. Based on the maximum possible holding, the sharp rise in the stock price could have increased the value of his investment by up to $15 million.However, the disclosures do not establish the exact number of shares Trump owned or account for any purchases or sales made in October and November. The filings provide holdings and transactions in broad value ranges rather than precise figures.According to the calculations based on these disclosures, Trump could have held as few as 32,000 Nvidia shares, worth approximately $5.3 million, which would translate into a gain of around $1.3 million following Monday's rally. The maximum estimate assumes that he bought the largest possible number of shares within each reported range and sold the smallest, while the minimum estimate assumes the opposite.The surge in Nvidia shares followed the company's decision to reinstate Huang, who had stepped aside following revelations about alleged extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence.Trump said he had been closely involved in the decision to bring Huang back to the company, claiming he had played a role in securing the outcome.“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them . I made the deal.”Nvidia's board said it had received input from “senior levels” of the US government before deciding to reinstate Huang. “Based on that input, the board is confident that Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said.Trump also publicly backed Huang's return, writing on social media: “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”In his CNBC interview, Trump said the prospect of losing Huang's expertise to China was a greater concern than the national security questions surrounding his reported personal relationships.“The bigger threat would be losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen. That would be a threat — to me that would be a far bigger threat,” he said, responding to a question about whether Huang's relationship with a woman reported to have links to Chinese intelligence posed a national security risk.Trump also said he had discussed Huang at length with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his visit to China last week. According to Trump, Xi had spoken highly of the Nvidia chief executive.“I know how good China is … and I said to a few people, you know, I know what (Chinese) President Xi is thinking because I would be thinking like, why don’t we make a deal with Jensen?”“President Xi was saying (Huang is) the most brilliant in the world at that business,” Trump said, recalling the conversation.“Nobody understands it but a guy like Jensen, they can’t copy it. It’s uncopyable,” Trump added.“You take a look at a little wafer, and you say the complexity of that China can’t copy. Nobody can copy… most chips now are obsolete, and they become obsolete very quickly.”Huang has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, who has been suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. Reports have also alleged relationships with two Nvidia employees. The Wall Street Journal report did not publicly identify the additional women or provide details of the relationships disclosed to the company's board.The board's decision to reinstate Huang followed a series of discussions and meetings, after which directors said they were satisfied with his candour and ability to lead the company. Nvidia also maintained that the input it received from senior US government officials had given it confidence that his return did not pose a national security risk.Huang returned to Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara on Monday, where he received a warm welcome from employees. Addressing staff, he thanked them and said he would be a “better CEO the second time around”.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: How past income could trigger higher Medicare premiums in 2027
articles.summary: New income brackets and premiums announced for Medicare users who  earn too much to qualify for the standard Part B and Part D premiums and pay surcharges.
articles.body:
Medicare costs will continue to whittle away at Social Security checks next year. And the more you earn, the more you pay.

Since 2007, a beneficiary's Part B monthly premium is based on his or her income. About 9% of Medicare users earn too much to qualify for the standard Part B and Part D premiums and must pay surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts (IRMAA).

The surcharge is calculated on a sliding scale with five income brackets topping out at $500,000 for individuals and $750,000 for joint filers. These figures change annually with inflation.

Calculations have a two-year lag time. Whether you pay a surcharge in 2027 depends on the income on your 2025 tax returns.

"Exceeding a cutoff by just a dollar will trigger that bracket's full surcharge," said Philip Moeller, a Medicare and Social Security expert.

Unfortunately, it's easy to trigger IRMAA when you first retire and have signed up for Medicare, due to the two-year look-back feature, or if you're enrolled in Medicare but still working full-time.

For 2027, these inflation-adjusted brackets start at above $112,000, up from $109,000 this year for single tax filers, and over $224,000 up from $218,000 for joint filers, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) announced last week.

For these beneficiaries, total monthly Part B premiums will range from $293 to $711.80.

Part D surcharges will range from $15.40 to $96.40.

Medicare Part B base premiums, which cover doctors, outpatient care, some home healthcare services, and durable medical equipment, will rise about 3.2% to $209.40 a month in 2027 . Tally that up and the total premium will be $2,512.80 a year for those not hit by surcharges.

The Medicare Part B premium is deducted from your Social Security checks before you receive them. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027 . Starting in January, the increase will add about $75 per month to the average retiree's check.

The annual deductible for all Medicare Part B beneficiaries increases to $292 in 2027, up $9 from $283 in 2026.

If you're enrolled in traditional Medicare, you also have a Part D drug plan. The 2027 Part D base premium is $36 per month on average, but yours could be higher.

The maximum annual out-of-pocket for Part D prescription drugs, including the deductible, will rise to $2,400 in 2027 from $2,100 in 2026.

The Part A inpatient hospital deductible that must be paid will also rise by $40 to $1,776, after which there are no charges for stays up to 60 days. It's unusual to be hospitalized for longer, but if you do, you will pay a daily coinsurance rate of $444, up from $434, for stays lasting between 61 and 90 days.

articles.title: Chip stocks led a $3 trillion comeback on Monday — now comes Turnaround Tuesday: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Nvidia and chip stocks sent the S&P 500 to its best day since April 2025. History says the next week is usually rocky.
articles.body:
Wall Street threw its biggest party in more than a year and a half on Monday. History says the cleanup could take a while.

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) jumped nearly 5%, its best day since April 2025 , and added about $3 trillion in market value. Only that April 9 rebound added more.

The spark was Nvidia ( NVDA ). Its board brought back Jensen Huang after 12 days , and the stock soared 31%, adding about $950 billion. That's the biggest one-day gain any company has ever posted , more than double the old record.

President Trump took a bow. "I don't think anybody could revive the stock like it's being revived right now," he said.

Chip stocks did the rest. All 62 in a Yahoo Finance basket rose, adding about $2 trillion a week after their worst week since 2001 . SK Hynix ( SKHY ) and Micron ( MU ) each jumped about 20%. Six companies, from Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) to Tesla ( TSLA ), added $100 billion or more.

Not everyone got an invitation. CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) fell 9% after agreeing to buy Zscaler ( ZS ) for $43.9 billion. Anthropic ( ANT ) slipped as its options and leveraged ETFs debuted , though General Catalyst managing director Madhu Namburi isn't worried. "I do believe this could be the first $10 trillion company," he said on Deirdre Bosa Live .

The old Wall Street saying that Tuesday undoes Monday has a point. In the 20 times since 1993 that the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened Monday 2% or more higher, it rose the next day only nine times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. By Friday, it was a coin flip.

Turnaround Tuesday is right on schedule, with S&P 500 futures ( ES=F ) down about 1% and Nasdaq-100 futures ( NQ=F ) off about 2%.

Patience usually paid. A year later, SPY was higher in 17 of the 20 cases, with a typical gain of about 26%.

The bad cases were really bad, though. In a quarter of them, SPY fell 12% or more within three months. Five of the 20 came in the fall of 2008.

The S&P 500 took just 33 trading days to go from a record to a correction, and only three of the 10 fastest drops like that became bear markets, Carson Group's Ryan Detrick noted . The catch is that 33 days also matches October 2007, the start of a bear market that more than halved the index.

Watch Friday's low, about 6,880 on the S&P 500. Half of those 20 big Mondays slipped back below the prior Friday's low within three months .

Naveen Rao, CEO of Unconventional AI, reached for an older comparison on Deirdre Bosa Live. "Nvidia is so big and baked into so much of the growth of the US right now," he said. "It was a little bit like the banking crisis. You know, back in the 2008 time frame."

articles.title: How fear of AI displacement is fueling a hiring recession
articles.summary: Workers are staying put in their jobs over concerns of AI displacement.
articles.body:
The US labor market has proved remarkably resilient in the post-pandemic era. But as anyone looking for a job can tell you, it's rough out there. Just getting your resume past AI screeners and in front of a real person is a small victory in itself.

What's been described as a hiring recession is a labor market that has low unemployment but also one that has settled into a low-hire, low-fire environment. One of the reasons workers are staying put and fewer people are being welcomed aboard is artificial intelligence.

After a surge in people quitting their jobs or switching careers during the pandemic, workers are settling back in. But the lower levels of churn, or workers moving between jobs, are especially evident in industries closer to AI, suggesting a connection between a lack of labor dynamism and concerns around the technology.

"Churn has fallen further below pre-pandemic levels in industries with greater AI adoption and automation potential, as workers increasingly stay put amid rising job insecurity," analysts at Goldman Sachs wrote in a research report published Monday.

Consistent with that finding, the analysts said, workers' perceptions of their job prospects have recently deteriorated. Young people especially are registering sharper pessimism, as they "likely feel more exposed to AI displacement risk."

Even as Wall Street and much of corporate America tout the productivity benefits of AI, how the technology will ultimately impact the American workforce is a topic of intense debate.

Just last week, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh kicked off a landmark hearing examining how AI could reshape US productivity and the job market, highlighting its potential to drive economic growth while warning that its risks could be costly if overlooked .

In the short term, AI is already influencing hiring decisions. Managers are streamlining teams and offloading some work to LLMs and specialty agents. And roles that used to go to junior-level employees are being folded into AI workloads.

And at the same time, AI has caused a chill in much of the workforce. According to Goldman's report, fears around AI displacement are keeping workers in place.

Because even if your salary hasn't gone up much, the fact that jobs are harder to get makes them all the more valuable.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is a walking moral hazard
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board faced an impossible choice: stand its ground, or bring Huang back, setting a precedent that bad behavior can be ignored if the fallout is big enough.
articles.body: “With the situation becoming more precarious by the day, I faced a choice: To step in with dramatic action, or to stand back and allow the irresponsible actions of some to undermine the financial security of all.” That was former President George W. Bush in a nationwide televised address from the White House on September 24, 2008. Lehman Bros. had failed a week earlier, the Federal Reserve bailed out mega-insurer AIG, and Bush was pushing for a $700 billion taxpayer-supported rescue fund to save the financial system from collapse. Bush acknowledged he was a well-known believer in free enterprise and favored letting companies go out of business as a consequence of their bad decisions. “Under normal circumstances, I would have followed this course. But these are not normal circumstances.” History is repeating itself. Jensen Huang’s irresponsible behavior forced his resignation from Nvidia, leaving a $1.5 trillion hole in Nvidia’s stock valuation and an angry president of the United States in its wake. The chipmaker’s board faced an impossible choice: stand its ground and risk continued fallout that had spread throughout the AI industry and the US government … or bring Huang back, setting a precedent that bad behavior could be ignored if the consequences were great enough. The board chose the latter. The Huang saga is the latest “moral hazard,” an economic argument that dates back more than a century but was prevalent among bailout skeptics during the financial crisis. The gist: Bailing out reckless behavior will lead only to even riskier business in the future if the recipient of the bailout understands it (or he) is too big to fail. “Every founder in America just watched what too big to fire looks like,” said Chris Gannett, founder and CEO of Gannett Partners, an executive coaching firm. Moral hazard The term “moral hazard” emerged in the late nineteenth century as a critique of insurance, according to Donald Light, a health policy researcher for Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine. Honest, responsible policyholders paying premiums to cover their genuine risks feared they were enabling bad actors to engage in reckless behavior, because those policyholders knew they’d be covered regardless of how irresponsible they may be. The term took on a new meaning in 1968, when economist Mark Pauly commented that moral hazard actually had nothing to do with moral or immoral behavior. Instead, he said people might seek more medical care if they’re insured because they’re acting with “rational economic behavior.” In other words: Moral hazard is simply a market force. Pauly’s moral hazard definition continues in the medical industry. But it took on broader economic significance in subsequent years – particularly during the global financial crisis. Opponents of taxpayer-funded bailouts held that rescuing institutions or even individual borrowers who took on excessive risk excused their irresponsible behavior. Worse, it could encourage those bad actors to make even more dangerous choices in the future, because it signaled they would not be allowed to fail regardless of the risk they took on. “We’re very aware of moral hazard, but our primary concern right now … is the stability of our financial system, the orderliness of our markets,” former Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson told ABC News in March 2008 after the government orchestrated JPMorgan Chase’s bailout of Bear Stearns. That’s the same calculus Nvidia’s board made when rehiring Jensen Huang. The company did not respond to a request for comment. Huang stands accused of some serious violations of corporate policy. He acknowledged an affair after reports of a relationship with a major customer – who is suspected of having Chinese intelligence ties – and he was reportedly in a relationship with an employee. But the board must act in the best interest of shareholders. And a 28% wipeout in market value since Huang resigned wasn’t exactly in shareholders’ best interest. Nvidia is also unique: critical to US national security interests, the de facto central bank for AI and building the technology underpinning the country’s economic growth for years to come. President Trump was breathing down the board’s neck. So, like Bush in 2008, Nvidia’s board held its nose and took the path it believed it needed to, even if it trampled on its previously held beliefs – and even if it risks more bad behavior in the future. “Anyone who is too big to fire can take on more risk than they should,” said Shivaram Rajgopal, professor of corporate governance at Columbia Business School. Moral clarity There’s a reason why bosses aren’t allowed to have sexual relationships with employees and customers: It creates a power dynamic in which the subordinate may feel required to keep sleeping with their superior to remain employed. Customers may feel the same obligation to remain in business with the company led by the person they’re in a relationship with. It’s ethically unambiguous, and similar relationships led to the downfall of many former CEOs, including leaders of American Apparel, Boeing, Intel, McDonald’s and Hewlett-Packard. Huang’s relationship with a potential foreign intelligence asset also remains a subject of an ongoing independent investigation commissioned by the board. “Espionage aside, a sexual relationship with a customer and a sexual relationship with a subordinate would each be grounds for dismissal with cause,” said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors. By restoring Huang to the helm, it signals that he’s beyond reproach. “It sends a bad message,” said Rajgopal. “It says Huang is above the law. He’s an imperial CEO.”

articles.title: Democrats just won large majorities — here’s how they can keep them
articles.summary: Will they address our looming fiscal crisis, or will they make it worse?
articles.body:
There is no sugar-coating the 2026 election. Republicans took one of the worst shellackings of any party since the Great Depression. Democrats are celebrating a Senate majority of 56 seats and a House majority of at least 258, with two House races still uncalled and two headed for runoffs. As long as President Trump is in the White House, expectations for the 120th Congress are low. But what longer-term fiscal effects are likely to follow for the 121st Congress and beyond? Serious commentary about the election rightly centers on the Trump administration’s involvement in Iran (and gas prices) and increased consumer costs related to tariffs. However, there is a third policy, which is equally relevant to Republicans and Democrats as it affects whoever is in the majority: federal deficits. Deficits add to the national debt, and affect credit, interest rates, inflation, and — critically — the cost of living for everyday Americans. No easy solution exists for the fiscal crisis facing America. Can we increase taxes? While younger and working-class Americans pay burdensome payroll taxes to fund Social Security and Medicare for their elders (plus state and local taxes, and property taxes), after deductions and credits, most have incomes that are below federal tax thresholds. So tax increases would fall on higher income individuals, who are the nation’s job-creators. Yet changes to tax rates are an ineffective solution. One need only observe historical federal revenue collection over time to understand how the incentives created by tax increases frustrate all attempts to simply jack them up and cash in. Despite large variations in income tax rates over the last 60 years, federal revenue has hovered consistently around its long term average of about 17 percent of gross domestic product (16.8 percent last fiscal year), and mostly within the narrow band of 16 to 19 percent. The rare departures from this range correspond more closely with economic conditions than tax rates — for example, the modestly higher income tax rates of the early Obama years did not prevent revenues from going as low as 14.5 percent of GDP as effects from the financial crisis played out. Meanwhile, other policies intended to close a potential tax gap — such as broadening the tax base or subjecting more middle and upper-middle class households to audits — are usually all political pain with no gain. Can we decrease spending? Congress has proven unwilling to do so under either party’s control. Average annual spending growth in inflation-adjusted dollars during Bill Clinton’s presidency was a positive 1.4 percent, even with three years of surpluses; growth under George W. Bush was 4.1 percent; growth under Barack Obama was 2.0 percent; growth during Trump’s first term and Joe Biden was 5.2 percent; and growth during fiscal 2026 was 2.0 percent. From the Clinton era to the present, spending as a percentage of GDP has ranged from 18 percent (in fiscal 2001) to 31 percent (fiscal 2020), averaging 21 percent. Hence, spending averaged about 4 percentage points of GDP more than our natural capacity to collect revenue. Spending cuts are politically unpopular, and more unpopular as spending gets more concentrated in popular mandatory spending programs like Social Security and Medicare. Can we monetize the debt? This leads to higher inflation, which reduces everyone’s wages and savings. Voters notice when this happens — in two successive elections, we have just seen each party cut down because of inflation. If the 2026 results were mainly a rejection of current policy (Iran and tariffs), Democrats should be cautious and Republicans should temper their depression. History shows there is often a rebound from such outcomes, as voting behavior tends to revert to the mean — as it did after the 1946, 1958, 1994 and 2010 wave elections, among others. In the 120th Congress, House Democrats will be just above their 2008 peak, which featured 257 House members, and very close to their 1993 majority of 259. Senate Democrats are below their 2008 peak of 59 senators, and near their 57-seat majority before the 1994 election. How will Democrats choose to exercise these strong majorities — and specifically will they address our looming fiscal crisis, or will they make it worse? For America to remain a prosperous land of opportunity, where talent and effort can transform individuals’ and families’ economic standing, the nation must return to Alexander Hamilton’s fiscally responsible course. The Hamiltonian norm — largely abandoned by Democrats and Republicans alike for the better part of 60 years — is to stabilize the buildup of debt with austerity in spending and revenue policy. Today’s fiscal crisis grows more acute with delayed application of the Hamiltonian norm and the looming insolvency of Social Security. If the coming Democratic Congress can find a middle-ground path to return to the Hamiltonian norm with President Trump — a path that both right-wing Republicans and left-wing Democrats can accept as fair — it could be transformational. Such a rare statesmanlike accomplishment could help Democrats defend their majority for a long time to come. But failure means that inflation and the cost of living will continue to rise faster than the offset-subsidies Congress will try to provide. That could mean another big electoral swing on the horizon. Democrats are therefore on the clock. Doug Branch spent a quarter-century working in Congress for Republican House members and senators and is a senior fellow at the nonprofit, non-partisan Fiscal Lab on Capitol Hill.
